fields.title: Fix agent surfaces causing over-filing and status narration
fields.description: Fix the spawn handoff wording that pushes agents to file cheap findings as new tasks, and the status-change output from task update that agents relay to the user as narration.
fields.notes: Rewording (2) was tried before and failed.
fields.analysis:
# The primary defect: test 1 reads as a purity test

Bullet 1 — "Could it reasonably be done now, inside the work already underway?
Do it" — **was** in the handoff. It is not missing. It was read and rejected,
and the rejection was reasonable on the wording: "inside the work already
underway" is a **topical membership** question. Asked of a stray id in a guide
paragraph while the task was `verb update`, the honest answer is "no, that is
not part of this task's subject" — so the session falls to the next branch.

`docs/guide/tasks.md` then hardens the topical read rather than softening it:

> "Reasonably, inside the work already underway" is a real bound, not a
> license. A drive-by that is *unrelated* to what you are changing stays a
> separate task…

So the guide makes bullet 1 about **kinship** while ED-1550 makes filing about
**arithmetic** — the file-to-close ratio. For a cheap, unrelated fix those pull
opposite ways, and kinship wins because it is the test actually printed at the
decision point.

This is a repeat, not a one-off. The same reasoning — "it wasn't a *pure*
example of the other task" — has been given before as the justification for
filing rather than folding. Purity is the wrong axis. What matters is what the
fix costs to make and to review, and whether carrying it in this diff would
mislead a reviewer; not whether it is a clean instance of this task's category.

**Proposed:** bullet 1 states the axis and names the failure mode, e.g.

    - Could it reasonably be done now? Do it — note it in the commit message
      and say so in your reply. The test is COST, not kinship: how big is the
      fix, and would carrying it here mislead whoever reviews the diff. Do not
      let purity get in the way of proficiency — "not a pure example of this
      task" is not a reason to file. A one-line fix in a file you already have
      open is cheaper to make than the task row describing it.

That keeps the real bound (a large or risky unrelated change still splits out,
for diff, land-coupling and revert-blast-radius reasons) while removing the
category test that currently decides it.

# Folding in is not done until the plan records it

A session that folds discovered work into the task already underway must also
**amend that task's plan and/or outcome** to say so. The commit message and the
reply to the user are both transient: the commit is found only by someone
already reading that diff, and the reply is gone the moment the session is
archived. The task row is what posterity reads, and a task whose plan describes
only its original scope is a lie about what shipped under it — which is the
same defect that made "reopening shipped work forces a re-read of the whole
plan to find the new part" a rule in the first place.

So the do-it-now branch has three obligations, not two: do the work, note it in
the commit, **and record the grown scope on the task**.

**This has a trap that must be spelled out in the instruction.** Writing plan
text onto a task in a terminal status re-specs it:

    $ endless task update E-2114 --text-file plan.md
    • Status: assumed -> revisit
    E-2114 was 'assumed'; plan text changed → status set to revisit
    (pass --keep-status to suppress for a typo/formatting-only edit)

and `revisit` cannot go back: reachable from `revisit` are untriaged,
submitted, underway, declined, obsolete — **not** `assumed`. So a session that
obeys the new rule the obvious way destroys the verification state its user just
granted, and the only way back is a full claim/verify cycle the user has to
re-close. Hit live on E-2114 while writing this analysis.

The instruction must therefore carry `--keep-status`, not merely mention that
it exists — and it is worth asking whether recording delivered scope on a done
task should be a re-spec at all, or whether `--keep-status` is the wrong
default for a plan edit that only appends history.

# Secondary: the handoff drops the framing and the override

`docs/guide/tasks.md` opens the discovery section with **"Filing is one of four
answers, not the default"** and closes it with an override:

> One case overrides test 1's bound: a drive-by you genuinely cannot complete
> the task without — a broken build, **a test that fails for an unrelated
> reason**. Fix the minimum that unblocks you even when it is otherwise out of
> scope, and say so explicitly in your report.

`internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/_mechanics.tmpl:28-36` compresses the
four tests into three bullets and keeps neither. `otherwise file it` is left as
the terminal branch, and nothing puts the filing *decision* in front of the
user.

# The missing branch: ASK, don't decide

The branch to add is not "tell your user and file nothing". A session that
decides unilaterally not to file is as wrong as one that files reflexively —
it just fails in the direction that loses real findings silently instead of the
direction that inflates the backlog. The agent has the context to explain a
finding; it does not have the standing to rule on whether that finding earns a
row.

So the branch is a **question**, and it has a shape:

- **Enough detail to understand the purpose, and no more.** What was observed,
  and why it would matter to someone who was not in this session. Not a repro
  transcript, not a diff, not a plan.
- **The case FOR filing.** What goes unfixed or unremembered if this is
  dropped; who trips over it next; whether it compounds.
- **The case AGAINST filing.** Review and scheduling cost; whether an existing
  task already owns the area; whether it is a symptom of something already
  filed; whether it is small enough that noticing it again later costs less
  than carrying the row.
- **A recommendation**, so the user is ratifying a judgement rather than doing
  the triage themselves.

The user answers; the session files or drops on that answer. This keeps
ED-1550's arithmetic — filing stays the exception — without making "drop it"
a decision the agent makes alone.

# Third: the override's condition contradicts its own example

The condition is "you genuinely cannot complete the task without"; the example
is "a test that fails for an unrelated reason". Those are not the same set — an
unrelated red test usually does *not* block completion. E-2114 landed clean
with `test_no_self_dev_ids` red for a reason that had nothing to do with it.

So even a session that reads the full guide finds the example matching and the
condition not matching, and falls through to filing. The condition wants
rewording around the *regression the session is obliged to run and report*,
not around being blocked.

# Live case

E-2114's project-wide regression turned up a stray self-dev id in
`docs/guide/orchestration.md` — one sentence, in a tree already open, in a
suite the session had just run. It was filed as E-2119 instead of folded in,
which cost an extra worktree, an extra task row, a partial-state `task claim`
error, and two round trips with Mike. E-2119 was then obsoleted and the fix
folded into E-2114 by hand.

# Constraint

Keep test 1's real bound intact. The guide is right that a *large* unrelated
drive-by inflates the reviewed diff, couples two changes into one land, and
widens a revert's blast radius. The fix is to change what the bound is measured
in — cost and reviewer confusion, not topical kinship — and to route the
residue to the user as a question rather than straight into `task add`.

---

# Second root cause: the status-change surface trains narration

Same session, different file, same shape — what the agent is told at a decision
point determines what it does next.

Every status-affecting `task update` prints two things: the field render
(`• Status: assumed -> revisit`) and an advisory naming `--keep-status`. Both
are addressed to the agent. The agent relays them to the user as if they were
news, which spends the user's attention — the scarcest resource in the loop —
on a completed, correct transition it can do nothing about.

This is not a first offence and not a wording problem. A comment beside the
`auto_untriage` emitter in `task_cmd.py` records a previous session diagnosing
the identical loop — *"observed four times in one session"* — and fixing it by
**rewording** the advisory. It did not take: the reworded line was relayed twice
more in this session alone. The stimulus is the presence of agent-addressed
output, not its phrasing, so a third rewrite would fail the same way.

## Fix, two halves, landed together

**1. Audience-gate the output.** Keep everything exactly as it is for a human
running the command interactively — the status change and both advisories are
genuinely useful there. For an agent, print only the field changes it asked
for. Nothing about status it did not ask about, and no advisory.

Reuse `agent_help.agent_view()`. That predicate is already the consolidated
answer to "is an agent reading this" — E-1966, E-2006 and E-2097 each folded a
competing spelling into it, so a fourth spelling is the specific mistake this
module's history warns against. `--help` and refusals already gate on it; the
status-change output becomes a third caller.

**2. Narrow the transition that fires under it.** A plan-text edit on a
terminal status (`confirmed` / `assumed` / `completed`) must not move the
status. Today it auto-flips to `revisit`, inferring "the work needs redoing"
from an edit that, on a finished task, usually records what shipped — which is
exactly the obligation the fold-in branch above now imposes.

No new flag for the inverse: `{From: Assumed, To: Revisit, Actor: ActorUser,
Label: "reopens — shipped work found wrong"}` already exists in
`internal/taskstatus/transitions.go`, alongside the same edge from `Confirmed`
and `Completed`. Reopening is already user-owned and already spelled
`--status revisit`; the defect is the system firing a user's edge on an
inference. Non-terminal statuses keep today's behaviour, where the auto-flip is
cheap and usually right.

## Why both, not either

Half 1 alone hides a transition the agent caused: it would silently knock a task
off `assumed` and not know. Half 2 alone leaves the field render and the
advisory in place for the agent to narrate. Together there is no wrong
transition to hide and nothing agent-addressed left to relay.

`--keep-status` itself survives untouched. Its other job — skipping the
re-triage model call on a cosmetic description edit — is a real spend control
and unrelated to this.

## Live case

Recording E-2114's grown scope in its plan — obeying the rule this very task
adds — flipped it `assumed → revisit`, and `revisit` cannot reach `assumed`
again. The verification Mike had granted an hour earlier was destroyed by the
act of documenting what shipped, and had to be walked back through
`underway → unverified` for him to re-close by hand.

## From the description

restate the axis as cost and reviewer confusion, add the missing branch that ASKS the user whether to file with pros and cons, and require the fold-in branch to record grown scope on the task.

keep all of it for a human, show an agent only the field changes it asked for, and stop a plan edit on a terminal status auto-flipping to revisit.

fields.title: Run database backups on a schedule with tiered retention
fields.description: Run database backups on a schedule rather than only before schema migrations, and replace count-based rotation with tiered retention: hourly for a day, daily for 30 days, weekly for a year.
fields.context:
Backups only run before a schema migration: _backup_db has exactly one caller, and the Go path fires only from the pre-apply step during land and from an explicit endless db backup.

So the newest backup can be weeks old — it was nine days stale when it was needed.

The docstring's 'if last backup is > 60 seconds old' reads like a frequency but is only a throttle on a rare event.
fields.analysis:
## Why this surfaced

A bulk edit needed undoing and the newest backup was nine days old. It was still
usable, but only by luck: nothing about the current design makes recency likely.

Evidence for the diagnosis, not just the symptom:

- `_backup_db` has one caller, commented "backup before any migration".
- The Go equivalent runs from the pre-apply step during land, and from an
  explicit `endless db backup`. Neither is a schedule.
- Sixty files on disk — the rotation cap — spanning three months. That is about
  one every day and a half, clustered around migrations rather than evenly.
- The newest is dated to the last schema change, which is exactly what
  backup-on-migration predicts.

The 60-second window in the docstring is a throttle so two migrations back to
back do not write two copies. It is not a cadence, and it reads like one.

## Time Machine is not the fallback

Worth recording, because it was tried first. A Time Machine snapshot of the live
database was torn — SQLite was mid-write, `PRAGMA integrity_check` failed, and
`.recover` reassembled rows wrongly: fields from one table appeared in another's
columns, and whole rows were missing. A filesystem-level copy of an open SQLite
database has no consistency guarantee.

The project's own backups are safe because they go through the SQLite backup API
and `VACUUM INTO`. That difference is the reason this job belongs in Endless
rather than being delegated to the machine's backup software.

## Shape

Follow the two jobs that already exist. A stable `JobName` (changing it orphans
the scheduling row and restarts history), a `Schedule` with an interval and a
`MaxBackoff`, registered so `session monitor` picks it up via the same RunDue
path. Unlike the model-calling jobs, this one costs no spend, so the interval is
governed by acceptable data loss, not by budget.

## Retention

Replaces keep-last-60-by-count, which is a count where it should be an age:

- hourly for 24 hours
- daily for 30 days
- weekly for a year

That is roughly 106 files at steady state. Retention must be evaluated by
timestamp tier, not list position, so a burst of migrations can no longer evict
the older tiers — the failure mode the current rotation has today.

## From the description

Register a backup job in the internal/jobs registry the way triagejob and minimizerjob do, so session monitor fires it on a schedule, and replace the keep-last-60-by-count rotation with tiered retention: hourly for 24 hours, then daily for 30 days, then weekly for a year.

fields.context: The guide still presents eswt as a shell helper: docs/guide/orchestration.md's shell-helpers table calls it '(Planned, not yet shipped.)', and docs/guide/index.md, docs/guide/help/_topics.md and docs/guide/help/shell-init.md list it beside esu as if a reader had it.
fields.analysis:
Scope boundary, so this is not folded into E-1428 by a later reader who sees 'eswt' in both.

E-1428 ('Rework endless task claim output') has four deliverables. A — fix the broken eswt reference — was delivered by E-2106, which deleted the whole 'choose one' block that carried it. B, C and D are open, and B is a live footgun with nothing to do with eswt: worktree_cmd still prints 'sandbox provisioned: ~/.cache/endless/sandboxes/<name>' as a line parallel to the worktree path, users cd into it, and every subsequent endless command then fails with 'Not in a registered project directory' (hit by Mike 2026-05-19). E-1428 also wants an 'endless worktree sandbox' verb to retrieve that path on demand, which does not exist. Folding B into a documentation task would bury it.

So: E-1428 keeps the command-OUTPUT work. This task is the guide PROSE, and it is the tail of E-1180 rather than of E-1428 — E-1180 proposed the helper, the guide documented the proposal, and obsoleting E-1180 is what makes the documentation wrong.

Related closures, for anyone reading the eswt trail: E-1180 obsolete (we will not ship it), E-1254 obsolete (its subject, claim's eswt line, was deleted by E-2106).

## From the description

Find every site with: grep -rn eswt docs/.

fields.title: Stop tmux spawns landing in the operator's frontmost session
fields.description: Stop spawned tmux windows opening in whichever session was most recently active by giving every new window an explicit target, in the product and in the test that triggers it.
fields.context: tests/test_task_claim_worktree.py::test_claim_binds_sibling_claude_session proves it: it calls the attended claim path and opens real tmux windows, each launching a Claude Code trust prompt, in the operator's live session during `just test`.
fields.analysis:
# An untargeted `tmux new-window` lands in whoever's session is in front

## The product defect

Anything in endless that shells out to `tmux new-window` without a
`-t <session>` target lands the window in the most-recently-active tmux session.
On this machine that is Mike's live `active` session. On a downstream user's
machine it is whatever they happen to have in front — a stray window appears in
an unrelated session with no indication of where it came from or what it belongs
to.

Find the call sites with `grep -rn 'new-window' src/ internal/`. One is in
`src/endless/session_cmd.py` (a `new-window -d -c <worktree>` invocation); the
others are the Go spawn path in `internal/spawnlaunchcmd` (`tmux_driver.go` and
`spawn_window.go`). The Go one is downstream of `emit_event`, so it is invisible
from the Python side and will not be found by reading the caller.

## The reproducer, which is a second and separable defect

`tests/test_task_claim_worktree.py::test_claim_binds_sibling_claude_session` is
the only test in that file that calls the ATTENDED path — `claim_item(tid)` with
no `unattended=True`. It patches `_resolve_session_id_with_prompt` to return a
fake sibling session id and then does real claim work: `create_task_worktree` in
a tmp project, an event emit, and whatever the spawn path does next.

So `just test` opens real tmux windows in the operator's live session, each
launching a Claude Code trust prompt for a pytest tmp_path. Observed while
E-1957 was running the suite: `pytest-173/174/175/177`, directory name truncated
by pytest to `test_claim_binds_sibling_claud0`, and worktree `e-1` because each
test gets a fresh isolated database in which the seeded task is always id 1.

## Why the existing isolation does not help

`tests/conftest.py` already deletes `TMUX` and `TMUX_PANE` to keep the resolver
helpers off the real server. That only stops code which BRANCHES on the env var.
The tmux CLI reaches the running server through the default socket regardless,
so anything that shells out unconditionally is unaffected.

## Fix the cause, not only the trigger

A test-only fix — making the test unattended, or stubbing the spawn boundary —
stops the noise here and leaves the untargeted `new-window` intact for every
downstream user. Both halves are needed:

- every `new-window` call site takes an explicit target;
- the test gets its own tmux server on a private socket (`tmux -L <name>`, torn
  down afterwards) or a stubbed boundary, so a test can never reach the
  operator's live session again.

## Provenance

Surfaced during E-1957, which ran the project-wide pytest suite as a regression
step. Diagnosis by the session in worktree e-2106, which traced the tmp_path
name back to the test and identified the two candidate call sites.

## From the description

Both halves need fixing — a test-only fix leaves the product defect intact.

fields.title: Return full field bodies from task show --json
fields.description: Return full field bodies from task show --json by default, with an opt-in brief mode that truncates, so null means only empty rather than also withheld.
fields.notes: E-1601 specified that deliberately; this task revisits it for the machine format only.
fields.context: A consumer that does not pass a display flag reads a populated task as empty, and 'null' means both 'empty' and 'withheld' — indistinguishable for description, which has no _chars companion.
fields.analysis:
## Observed

    endless task show E-1347 --json --db main

returns, in the same object:

    "analysis": null
    "analysis_chars": 6503

The field has 6503 characters. The machine format says it is null.

`--analysis --json` (or `--all-fields --json`) returns the body. So the display
flags that gate the HUMAN renderer are also gating the JSON payload.

## Why this is worse than the terminal case

The terminal renderer is honest about hiding: it prints
`Analysis: 6503 chars (--analysis to display)`, which tells a reader both that
content exists and how to get it. That placeholder is the entire reason a human
can recover.

`--json` has no placeholder. `null` is the same value the field carries when it
is genuinely empty, so a consumer cannot distinguish "no analysis" from
"analysis withheld pending a flag you did not pass". The `_chars` sibling
contradicts it, but only for a consumer who already suspects the problem — which
is exactly the consumer who does not need the warning.

A machine format that silently omits populated content is not a rendering
choice; it is wrong output. Display flags belong to the display.

## Inconsistency in the sibling keys, same call

    description       557 chars returned    description_chars: null
    analysis          null                  analysis_chars: 6503
    text              null                  text_chars: null
    outcome           null                  outcome_chars: null

`description` is always returned and its `_chars` is null. `analysis` is
withheld and its `_chars` is populated. So neither the body nor the count can be
relied on to indicate presence, and the two disagree about which is
authoritative. Under `--all-fields --json` the same task reports `text` as an
empty string and `outcome` as null — two spellings of absent, in one object.

## Direction

`--json` should carry every field's real value, always: content when there is
content, and one consistent spelling of absent when there is none. The display
flags (`--analysis`, `--text`, `--outcome`, `--all-fields`, `--no-description`)
should affect only the human renderer.

If a caller genuinely needs a lighter payload, that is a separate, explicit
opt-out — and it should still be distinguishable from empty. Note that `--llm`
is a second machine-facing format and needs the same audit; it was not measured
here beyond confirming it is JSON-shaped.

Decide what a consumer should see, then make the `_chars` keys agree with it —
they are either redundant (drop them) or they are the presence signal (populate
them uniformly). Today they are neither.

## Blast radius

Any agent or tool reading task content through `--json` sees empty fields for
populated ones and proceeds on a partial record. This is the machine-facing
instance of the failure that produced the `--text` to `--all-fields` sweep: the
design content of a task sitting behind a flag the reader did not know to pass.
There the reader was a human who could at least see the placeholder.

## From the description

Fix: --json returns full bodies by default, and a new --brief[=N] opts into a light payload by truncating to 256 chars with an ellipsis rather than omitting, so a populated field is always a string and null means only 'empty'.

fields.title: Share one per-repo patch-id index across worktrees
fields.description: Share one per-repo patch-id index across all worktrees, appended as the base grows, so the exact unlanded probe stops recomputing base patch-ids per worktree; build it only if cache misses hurt.
fields.context: The exact unlanded probe's cost is dominated by computing patch-ids for every commit the base gained since a worktree's fork, and every worktree recomputes them against substantially the same base history — measured 584ms for e-1077 against 135 worktrees that share one main.
fields.analysis:
range-diff's similarity pairing, which is what catches a conflict-resolved landing, would run as a second stage over only the unmatched residue.

Deferred from E-2111 deliberately: with the verdict computed by a background job and a settled verdict surviving base movement, every miss is off the critical path and cold-miss storms are small.

Measure first; build only if misses actually hurt.

Invalidation rides the same base-tip watermark E-2111 introduces.

fields.title: Compute the exact unlanded verdict in one background job
fields.description: Compute the exact verdict on whether a branch holds unlanded work in one background job writing a shared cache, and have the reaper and display surfaces read it instead of re-probing.
fields.notes: This task conforms to decision ED-1589.
fields.context:
The exact 'does this branch hold work the base lacks?' probe (git range-diff, measured 584ms per worktree) is recomputed by every consumer on every tick: the reaper on five hook branches including PreToolUse and PostToolUse, and every session monitor pane re-probing every rendered row every two seconds.

Restores agreement between the reaper, the diamond marker and 'task unsettled' about what landed, which the E-2087 hotfix broke on purpose, and closes the reclamation leak it accepted.
fields.analysis: Delete the five hook-path reaper calls; the reaper keeps its existing trigger, the post-land sweep worktree land already runs, and gains an exact condition 4 that reads the cache.

fields.title: Rebase idle worktree branches onto the base on a cadence
fields.description: Rebase each idle worktree branch onto the base branch periodically so its merge base moves forward, shrinking the unlanded probe's cost and making later lands fast-forwards.
fields.notes:
E-1881's counterpart and the other half of keeping worktrees in sync: E-1881 moves endless-managed metadata commits UP to main, which is what lets a worktree settle and become reclaimable;

Blocked by E-1881 rather than merely related: without it the branch still holds metadata commits main changed independently, so a rebase hits exactly the conflicts E-1882 exists to resolve by hand.
fields.context: That collapses the range the exact unlanded probe pays for — its cost is proportional to how far the base drifted since the fork, not to what the branch holds — and makes a later land a fast-forward.
fields.analysis:
## Why this is the other half, not a duplicate of E-1881

The two sync jobs fix opposite sides of the same subtraction, and neither
subsumes the other.

- **E-1881, worktree -> main.** Moves endless-managed metadata commits (plans,
  analyses, ledger) UP. Those commits are the bulk of what makes a long-lived
  branch read as holding unlanded work, so removing them is what lets a worktree
  SETTLE and become reclaimable. It does nothing for probe cost; by growing main
  faster it slightly increases the cost for every other worktree.
- **This task, main -> worktree.** Rebases an idle branch onto the base, moving
  the merge base forward. That collapses the range the exact unlanded probe
  actually pays for, and it settles nothing by itself.

## The cost model this exploits

The exact probe (`unlandedCommits`, via `git range-diff`) costs in proportion to
how far the base has drifted since the fork — the patch-ids it computes are for
every commit the BASE gained, not for what the branch holds. Measured on this
repo: a worktree 2251 commits behind costs 2.1s; e-1077, 648 commits behind,
costs 584ms. A branch sitting at the base tip has an empty base range and costs
almost nothing.

So this does not make the algorithm cheaper — it removes the input that makes
the algorithm expensive.

## Why E-1881 blocks this rather than merely relating to it

Without E-1881, the branch still holds metadata commits that main changed
independently. Rebasing then hits exactly the overlapping-edit conflicts that
E-1882 (`endless worktree reconcile`) exists to resolve by hand — the scenario
that cost ~20 minutes of manual investigation during the E-1537 land. E-1881
running continuously leaves little on the branch to conflict with, which is what
makes an unattended rebase safe.

## Hard constraint

Only worktrees with NO live session and no process holding cwd inside, via the
same `WorktreeInUse` predicate the reaper shares with the other destructive
path (E-1947). A rebase rewrites history underneath whoever is sitting in the
directory. This is not a tunable.

## Interactions

- **E-2128.** A rebase moves the branch tip, invalidating that worktree's cached
  verdict. They compose rather than fight: the recompute is cheap by
  construction, because the drift it would have measured is what the rebase just
  removed.
- **E-1109** (`merge-vs-rebase` config preference) decides the mechanism. Rebase
  matches what `worktree land` already does; a merge is gentler but leaves merge
  commits on every task branch.

## From the description

Hard constraint: idle worktrees only, via the WorktreeInUse predicate the reaper shares with the other destructive path (E-1947).

fields.title: Propagate an interrupted git child through DefaultBranch
fields.description: Propagate an interrupted git child out of default-branch resolution instead of collapsing it into an unresolved-branch error that is recorded as a fault and cached for every later probe.
fields.notes: the misclassification E-2113 removed for ERR-0010, surviving under a different error code.
fields.context: E-2113's guards on the two default-branch fault recorders are correct but unreachable until the resolver stops swallowing the interrupt.

fields.description: Render the decisions linked to a task in task show's relations block alongside task links, so a session reading its own task can see which decisions bind it.
fields.context:
endless task show renders task-to-task relations only.

A decision linked to a task — documents, implemented_by, relates_to — is visible from decision show but invisible from the task, so a session reading its own task cannot see which decisions bind it.

ED-1589 links to E-2128 as implemented_by and does not appear anywhere in 'task show E-2128'.

This is why tasks acquired the prose habit of opening with 'Implements ED-NNNN': the banner was carrying information the view refused to render.

That convention is now banned, which makes this gap load-bearing rather than cosmetic.
fields.analysis: Check task show --all-fields and the JSON output for the same omission.

fields.title: Require an explicit DB context and state it on every read
fields.description: Require an explicit per-invocation flag before a command opens the database, instead of guessing the context from the working directory, and have every read state which context it used.
fields.context: Both halves are one omission: monitor.guardWorktreeDBContext already refuses to open the DB inside a self-dev worktree with no explicit context, and already names the remedy, but dbContextExplicit() is 'dbContextDir != "" || dbPathOverride != ""' and main.go calls SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox() for every subcommand, so CWD satisfies a gate whose own comment says only a flag counts.
fields.analysis:
One cause, two halves: the scope a command uses is inferred from ambient state and never declared. Stop the guess, and state the answer. Filed as one task per ED-1550 rule 3.

== HALF 1: stop the guess ==

The sibling comment on dbContextDir forbids exactly this for XDG_CONFIG_HOME: 'Deliberately NOT satisfied by XDG_CONFIG_HOME: an env var can be exported once and silently route every later command to the wrong DB -- the exact failure mode the gate exists to kill. Only a per-invocation flag (or the hook's ForceRealDB) counts as explicit.' CWD does the same thing without even an export, and the guard accepts it.

The distinction is already modelled. dbContextFromFlag exists to separate an explicit --config-dir from a cwd-self-detected sandbox, and SelfDetectWorktreeSandbox deliberately calls setDetectedContextDir rather than SetDBContextDir so it will not suppress the hook/tmux main pin. Everything needed is present; dbContextExplicit() simply reads the wrong one of the two. Detection should decide WHERE TO LOOK; only a flag should decide THAT YOU MAY OPEN IT -- config and log routing can stay CWD-derived without granting permission to read or write rows.

Blast radius. Unaffected: hooks (ForceRealDB sets dbPathOverride), tmux / session-status / project-status (PinMainDB), verify suites and tests (--config-dir), and the sandbox subcommand (no DB init). Affected deliberately: un-flagged DB-opening invocations from inside a self-dev worktree, including the Python CLI when no --db was passed. OPEN QUESTION for the plan: does the Python CLI keep self-detecting and thread --config-dir itself, or must it too refuse? That is the ergonomic call and the reason this needs a plan rather than a one-line patch.

== HALF 2: state the answer ==

Owner decisions, taken 2026-09-11:
  1. Announce ALWAYS, on every read -- not only when the scope was inferred rather than named. Repetition is cheaper than a rule about when to look.
  2. Machine formats carry it as a FIELD IN THE PAYLOAD, not on stderr.

Decision 2 departs from rowcap.echo_footer's precedent, which sends the omission trace to stderr for --json/--tsv so '| jq' will not choke, and the departure is deliberate: that footer is prose COMMENTARY ABOUT an answer and would corrupt a payload, whereas the store a result came from is DATA ABOUT THE RESULT and belongs in it. For array payloads the field goes per-row (non-breaking; rows such as list-live's already carry project_id); for object payloads, once at top level. --llm and human output carry it in-band on stdout; session list already prints 'Sessions - project: probe' and that header is the precedent.

Why stderr was rejected, from the agent's own account: in the incident session it wrote 2>/dev/null, 2>&1 | head, | tail -5 and 2>&1 | python3 -c repeatedly, each of which discards stderr or buries it under a truncation. Ranked by what actually reaches an agent: (1) a field in the structure it parses, near-unmissable because it destructures it; (2) stdout it quotes back, high, because what is in the pasted text is in the claim; (3) stderr, moderate and hardest to see when the command SUCCEEDED and returned the wanted data; (4) documentation read at session start, near zero at the moment of error. Hook stderr is weaker still -- it arrives as system-reminder text an agent is told to treat as background.

Scope note. The DATABASE half is self-dev-only: apply_db_choice refuses --db outright on a non-self-dev project because such a project has one DB. The PROJECT half reaches everyone -- session list, session-query list-live and project-status all scope to 'the project enclosing cwd', so a command run from a worktree, a sibling checkout, or a directory inside a different registered project answers about a project the caller did not name.

== THE INCIDENT ==

A session working E-2105 ran 'endless-go session-query list-live --project-root <main checkout>' from its worktree. --project-root named the main checkout; the binary silently answered from the worktree sandbox, returning 2 rows where main holds 59. The session reported it to the owner as a probable product defect, having also unset XDG_CONFIG_HOME in the belief that this was what selected the sandbox. It then ran the same command against two different binaries, got identical output, and read the agreement as corroboration -- a sound control for 'did my change alter this?' and none at all for 'is this number right?'. The refusal that would have ended this at the first command was already written and already unreachable.

## From the description

Fix both: require dbContextFromFlag (already tracked, never consulted) so only a per-invocation flag authorises opening the DB, and make every read state the database and project it answered from.

fields.title: Make every DB read state its database and project
fields.description: Make every read command state the database and project it answered from: a payload field in machine formats and in-band for agent and human output, always rather than only when surprising.
fields.context:
Endless read commands resolve their scope -- which database, which project -- from ambient context and then omit it from the answer, so a caller quotes a truthful answer about something they did not name.

session list already prints 'Sessions - project: probe' and that header is the precedent; session-query list-live's JSON carries project_id but never names the database.

fields.title: Install Endless's Claude Code hooks per project
fields.description: Install Endless's Claude Code hooks in each project's own settings at project init instead of machine-wide user settings, and migrate off the user-level entries.
fields.context: Endless installs its hooks machine-wide in the user's Claude Code settings, so every session in every directory invokes endless-go on every hooked event — including projects that will never use Endless.
fields.analysis:
`endless setup claude-hook` writes Endless's seven hook entries into the USER's
Claude Code settings, machine-wide. So every Claude Code session on the machine,
in any directory, invokes `endless-go hook claude` on every hooked event —
including in projects that have nothing to do with Endless, and will never have
anything to do with it.

Three reasons that is the wrong level, and the third is the load-bearing one:

- PERFORMANCE. A process spawn per hooked event, per session, per project on the
  machine, to do nothing.
- COMPLEXITY. It forces a runtime bypass to exist and stay correct —
  `agentenv.Supported`, `shouldSkipForWorktree`, the unregistered-project path.
  That machinery exists only because the hook is reachable where it should not
  be.
- ROBUSTNESS. A bug in the bypass means Endless acts on a project that never
  opted in. A hook that was never registered cannot have that bug. Removing the
  reachability is strictly stronger than gating it, and "the gate works today"
  is not an argument against removing it.

It also makes Endless opt-OUT rather than opt-in. `monitor.ProjectIDForPath`
auto-registers any directory a session runs in as an active project — 52 rows
on the development machine as of 2026-09-11, including the home directory. That is downstream of the
hook firing, so scoping the hook subsumes it rather than competing with it.

WHAT TO BUILD

`project init` writes the hook entries into the project's own
`.claude/settings.json`. The hook command is a committed, project-relative loader
script rather than an absolute path, so the committed file carries nothing
machine-specific: the loader locates `endless-go`, and when it cannot, tells
Claude to ask the user to approve installing it. The bootstrap cost is therefore
first-run-only, not permanent — which is what makes `git clone` and go real
rather than aspirational.

MIGRATION

The user-level entries must be removed, not merely supplemented: Claude Code
merges hooks across settings levels, so a tracked project would otherwise
double-fire every event.

CONSTRAINT — DO NOT FORECLOSE A USER-MACHINE LAYER

Endless is expected to split its database into a user-machine half (projects,
sessions) and a project half (tasks). When that lands, some hook
responsibilities may legitimately belong at the user-machine level — "which
session is this, which pane, is it alive" is user-machine; "does this session
hold a task, may it write" is project. The end state is plausibly BOTH levels.

This task scopes installation to the project and leaves the per-responsibility
partition to follow the DB work. It deliberately does NOT block on that split —
this is the easier of the two, and shipping it first does not constrain it.

## From the description

That forces a runtime bypass to exist and stay correct, when an unregistered hook simply cannot fire.

fields.title: Decide how to make folding a finding cheaper than filing it
fields.description: Decide which change actually makes an agent fold a finding into an existing task rather than file a new one, given filing is one command and folding is several, and what each option costs.
fields.context:
ED-1550 wants a finding folded into an existing task rather than filed as a new one, but the tooling inverts the incentive: filing is one command, folding afterwards is four plus a content merge, and the same-session root-cause hint fires only AFTER the task already exists.

Live case: a session filed two tasks for one cause, wrote the shared cause into the second task's own analysis, read the hint, answered it in prose, and filed anyway.

fields.title: Emit agent-facing output as TOON
fields.description: Emit agent-facing output from the Python CLI as TOON, defining the shape rules it applies: list versus detail commands, prose and empty fields, a shared key vocabulary, and no truncation.
fields.notes:
E-1504 sweeps 31 commands to offer an agent-facing text view; this settles what that view IS, and lands first so those renderings are written once rather than twice.

Discussed in session 539 as E-1504's peer and never filed.

See analysis.
fields.analysis:
## Why this is separate from E-1504, and blocks it

E-1504 sweeps 31 commands to offer an agent-facing text view. If the format is
not settled first, those 31 renderings get written twice — once ad hoc, once in
TOON. The format is the cheap thing to get right early and the expensive thing
to change late, so it lands first and E-1504 writes against it.

Discussed in session 539 alongside E-1504 ("two tasks, peers"); E-1504 was filed
and this one never was.

## Only the Python implementation is on the path

The agent-facing CLI is Python. Go owns database access and its JSON output —
`endless-go session-query worktree-unsettled`, `session-status --json` — is
internal plumbing consumed by Python, not by an agent reading output. So the
stable Python implementation is all this needs, and TOON's in-development Go
implementation is NOT a blocker for any agent-facing surface.

If Go ever emits agent-facing output directly, that is its own task and can use
whichever Go implementation is mature by then.

## Where TOON actually wins, and where it does not

Sorting the 31 commands by output shape splits them cleanly, and the split
determines the rules:

- **List-shaped** — `task list`, `task search`, `task next`, `task recent`,
  `task active`, `task landed`, `task unsettled`, `decision list`, `epic list`,
  `session status`, `session list`, `session search`, `session history`,
  `worktree list`, `verb list`, `phrase list`, `project status`. Arrays of
  uniform objects: TOON declares the fields once and emits one row per record
  instead of repeating every key on every row. This is the whole reason to adopt
  it.
- **Detail-shaped** — `task show`, `decision show`, `epic show`, `session show`,
  `worktree show`, `worktree current`, `worktree diagnose`. One object dominated
  by long free-text fields (description, analysis, plan). TOON's tabular saving
  does not apply; the win here is small and the format must simply not make
  prose worse.

## What the plan has to settle

1. **Dependency or in-house emitter.** Endless has three Python runtime
   dependencies today (click, inquirerpy, tabulate). Adding a fourth for TOON is
   a real posture change; writing a small emitter avoids it but owns the format's
   edge cases. Decide deliberately, not by reflex.
2. **How prose fields render.** A task description is multi-line text inside a
   record. Whatever TOON does with embedded newlines has to be legible and
   unambiguous when a title or description contains delimiters.
3. **Empty and default fields.** The `session status` JSON emits
   `blocked_by_n: 0`, `replaced_by: []`, `duplicates: []`, `hidden: false` on
   every row. Omitting defaults is the single largest saving across 31 commands,
   but in a tabular format the field list is declared once, so "omit" means
   something different than it does per-record. Resolve this explicitly.
4. **Shared key vocabulary.** `status`, `phase`, `owner` should mean the same
   thing in every command's output so the vocabulary is learned once.
5. **No truncation.** The human view cuts titles at terminal width. For an agent
   that is unrecoverable loss costing a second call, so agent output carries full
   values regardless of length.
6. **Glyph-encoded signals become explicit fields.** `session status` encodes
   ownership as `●` versus `⟳` and nothing else; an agent view without an
   explicit ownership field cannot tell this session's work from another
   session's. That failure is recorded on E-1504.

## Not in scope

Auto-selecting agent output when an agent invokes a command, plus the
counterpart flag that forces the human view. Its own task, after E-1504.

## From the description

Only the stable Python implementation is needed: Go's JSON is internal plumbing consumed by Python, not read by an agent, so TOON's in-development Go implementation blocks nothing.

fields.title: Write task doc mirrors to main, then consolidate them
fields.description: Write each task's human-readable doc mirror straight to main instead of the task branch, drain existing mirror commits off branches, then consolidate the mirrors into one directory per task.
fields.context:
Endless writes a task's content twice: the ledger entry, enforced to land on main only, and a human-readable mirror under .endless/plans|analyses|outcomes|decisions, which goes to the task BRANCH and waits for a land.

Measured over 133 worktrees: 123 of the 139 genuinely-unlanded commits are doc-mirror commits, and 44 of 56 unlanded worktrees are unlanded only because of them.
fields.analysis:
## The asymmetry nobody decided

Endless writes a task's multiline content twice:

1. The **ledger entry** — authoritative, and ENFORCED to land on the main
   checkout only. `commitPaths` refuses to write one anywhere else, and
   `worktree land` hard-refuses a branch-side ledger commit as corruption.
2. The **mirror** — `.endless/{plans,analyses,outcomes,decisions}/<ID>.md`,
   human-readable, which goes to the task BRANCH whenever a worktree exists and
   waits for a land to reach main.

Two halves of one write, on two different paths, with two different latencies.
Nobody decided that. It accreted: E-1525's goal was that the file was left
UNTRACKED and so never reached main at all, and committing it on the branch was
the nearest fix to hand. The goal was "get it into git", not "get it onto the
branch".

## What it costs, measured

Measured 2026-09-14 over 133 worktrees, using the content-based probe that
actually drives the diamond marker and reclaimability — not `rev-list`, which
counts by SHA and reports 890 where the real number is 139:

| | |
|---|---|
| worktrees unlanded by content | 56 |
| unlanded commits they hold | 139 |
| of those, doc-mirror commits | 123 |
| of those, real work | 9 |
| worktrees unlanded ONLY because of doc mirrors | 44 |

So 79% of the worktrees that read as holding unlanded work do so because
Endless put its own bookkeeping on their branch.

## Why this is the cause, not the symptom

E-1881 proposes a background job that sweeps those commits from each branch up
to main. That automates the cleanup. This removes the need for it: the mirror
follows the ledger to main at write time, and 123 of the 139 commits never
exist. Under ED-1550 that makes this the cause and E-1881 step 1 the symptom.

## Stop materializing into worktrees, too

`task update` is the only writer of these files and `task show` is the read
path, so a worktree copy is needed for neither. It is needed for browsing on
github.com — which main satisfies.

What a worktree copy DOES do is invite an agent to hand-edit content the
database owns, which is the same failure `.endless/LESSONS.md` needed a CLAUDE.md
rule to prevent. A file that is not there cannot be hand-edited. Materialize
once at worktree creation if browsability in the checkout is wanted, and let a
rebase refresh it; never write it again from `task update`.

The tempting middle option — write the worktree copy but leave it uncommitted —
is exactly what E-1525 removed. It makes every worktree permanently dirty, which
trips land's modified-worktree guard and pushes another hundred worktrees into
reading as modified.

## Prior decisions checked, and why neither blocks this

**ED-1169** considered "(a) auto-commit silently, (b) commit on the new task
branch" and chose refuse-with-recommendations, because "auto-commit hides
intent". It does not block this: it governs a plan file a HUMAN left uncommitted
in main at claim time. A mirror Endless authored is not anyone's hidden intent —
and `events.CommitDoc` / `_commit_doc_on_main` already auto-commit exactly these
files to main today, whenever no worktree exists. This makes the existing
behaviour the only behaviour.

**ED-1580** is rejected and must not be cited for this. Its rejection reason is
a caution worth heeding here: "over-generalized from one measurement... bundles
three claims."

## Two things the implementation has to settle

**`commitPaths` has no retry.** There is no `index.lock` handling anywhere in
`internal/events`; concurrent writers fail hard. `land` carries
`LAND_MAX_RETRIES = 8` for precisely this, so the discipline exists in the
codebase and simply is not on this path. Adding writers to main raises the
failure rate of something that already fails hard, so a retry belongs with this
change even if a proper serialization layer comes later.

**Orphan-branch recovery loses an input.** `_reconcile_orphan_plan` reads the
branch's committed copy (`git show <branch>:<plan>`) and compares it against
`tasks.text`, then asks the operator which to keep. That mismatch can only arise
BECAUSE the plan is on the branch. Once it is not, the code largely stops having
a job — re-examine it here rather than leaving it to rot, the same way E-1881
proposes re-examining E-1882.




# Absorbed from E-2138 — consolidating task content under .endless/tasks/e-NNNN/

## The convention already exists

`.endless/tasks/e-NNNN/` is already in use — 238 entries today, holding each
task's `verify.sh` beside the shared `_harness.sh`, `_guard.sh` and `CLAUDE.md`.
This consolidates the rest of a task's content into the directory that already
belongs to it, rather than inventing a layout:

```
.endless/tasks/e-2128/plan.md       <- .endless/plans/E-2128.md      (432 files)
.endless/tasks/e-2128/analysis.md   <- .endless/analyses/E-2128.md   (146 files)
.endless/tasks/e-2128/outcome.md    <- .endless/outcomes/E-2128.md   (134 files)
.endless/tasks/e-2128/verify.sh     (already there)
```

Decisions are NOT task-scoped — `ED-NNNN` has no owning task — so
`.endless/decisions/ED-NNNN.md` stays where it is. The restructure is for
task-scoped content only.

## Why now, beyond tidiness

**It fixes an allowlist that has already gone stale once.** E-1881's step 1 has
to name the directories holding task content. Its description, written
2026-08-04, names `plans`, `analyses` and `db-ledger` — and by the time it was
read on 2026-09-14 the real set was plans, analyses, outcomes and decisions,
while db-ledger had become wrong (those commits are orphans to drop, never
content to push up). Every future content type repeats that.

After this, the allowlist is one glob — `.endless/tasks/e-*/*.md` — and a new
content type needs no change to it, ever.

**It fixes a casing split.** `E-2128.md` inside `e-2128/` today. `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md`
already warns that a hand-written path "gets that wrong silently on a
case-insensitive filesystem and loudly on everyone else's".

## The two-lifecycle question, and why it is not a problem

Blocked by E-2137 for a reason. With mirrors written to main and not
materialized into worktrees, a worktree's `.endless/tasks/e-NNNN/` holds only
`verify.sh` — branch-authored, lands with the task — while main's holds that
plus the `.md` files Endless wrote there directly.

That is not split-brain, because there is no stale copy in the worktree to
disagree with main. It is one directory that is fuller on main than on a branch,
which is exactly what `.endless/db-ledger/` already is.

Done in the other order it WOULD be split-brain: a stale `plan.md` sitting next
to a live `verify.sh`, with nothing telling a reader which is authoritative.
That is the whole reason for the blocker.

What remains is documentation: `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md` must say which files in
that directory are the task's to write and which are Endless's.

## The migration, and what it collides with

A rename on main is a modify/delete conflict for any branch holding a commit at
the old path. Measured 2026-09-14: 51 worktrees hold 316 doc-mirror commits at
old paths, so the conflicts are real — but they are mechanical, and almost all
are the add/add shape where both sides are byte-identical (125 of 134 such files
had identical content on branch and main).

Two things reduce it rather than waiting for a quiet moment that never comes,
since there are always tasks underway:

- E-2137 landing first stops NEW doc-mirror commits reaching branches at all.
- `endless worktree sync` (E-1881) rebasing the fleet afterwards delivers the
  new layout, and a worktree holding no doc-mirror commits rebases cleanly.

The residue is each session resolving one mechanical conflict at its next
rebase, which is what the session-broadcast task exists to make humane.

## Tested: git's directory-rename detection misplaces content across tasks

Measured on a scratch repository 2026-09-14, not assumed. Two shapes, opposite
outcomes:

**A branch that MODIFIES a file main renamed rebases cleanly.** Git follows the
rename and lands the edit at the new path. No conflict.

**A branch that ADDS a file at the old path does not.** With
`.endless/plans/E-0.md` renamed to `.endless/tasks/e-0/plan.md` on main, a branch
adding `.endless/plans/E-2.md` rebased to:

```
.endless/tasks/e-0/E-2.md      <- E-2's plan, inside task e-0's directory
.endless/tasks/e-0/plan.md
.endless/tasks/e-2/plan.md
```

Git's directory-rename detection treated `.endless/plans/` as having become
`.endless/tasks/e-0/` and applied that to every new file in it. It raised a
conflict rather than doing this silently, but that IS the resolution it offers,
and `Endless: add plan for E-N` is the most common commit shape on these
branches.

`.endless/plans/` does not rename to one directory. It fans out to 432, and git
picks whichever one it detected.

**This is why E-2137 blocks this task, and the blocker is load-bearing rather
than an ordering preference.** E-2137's drain removes doc-mirror commits from
branches, so there is no new-file-at-an-old-path left for rename detection to
misplace. A branch that only ever MODIFIED such a file was always safe.

For any branch still holding doc commits when this runs — one whose worktree was
in use during the drain, so it was correctly skipped — the migration must either
re-drain it first or disable rename detection for that rebase
(`-X no-renames`). Do not let git guess: the guess puts one task's content in
another task's directory.

## From the description

Phase A writes the mirror to main at write time, stops materializing mirrors into worktrees, and drains the 123 commits off branches — which makes E-1881's step 1 unnecessary rather than automated.

Phase B, absorbed from E-2138, then consolidates the files into .endless/tasks/e-nnnn/<type>.md, the directory that already holds each task's verify.sh, replacing a directory allowlist that has already gone stale once with a single glob.

The order is not optional: git's directory-rename detection places a branch's new file inside another task's directory, so the drain must precede the rename.
